title: Judicial Activism & Restraint
lead: ==‘Judicial activism on the theory of jurisprudence called Sociological Jurisprudence arms the judiciary with wide legislative and executive powers’ — Justice Katju.== From resetting spectrum auctions to setting timelines for Governors, judicial activism is India's judicial reality — sometimes necessary, sometimes an overkill.

sections.title: Impact on Democracy & Separation of Powers

head: Positive
Negative
rows: ==Filling legislative gaps== — Vishaka guidelines on workplace harassment
==Accountability issues== — judges lack an electoral mandate
==Protecting vulnerable groups== — Right to Food litigation
==Institutional overlap== — courts assume administrative roles (Delhi Pollution Monitoring Committee, 2021)
==Executive accountability== — [[Vineet Narain v. UoI (1997)]] directing CBI autonomy
==Resource mismanagement== — courts lack policy-implementation expertise (Swachh Bharat directives)
==Innovative remedies== — continuing mandamus in environmental cases
==Judicial populism== — ban on liquor sale along highways
==Rights expansion== — privacy as a fundamental right (2017)
==Democratic erosion== — [[NCT of Delhi v. UoI (2018)]] redefining federal powers
==Inconsistency== — ad hoc rulings create legal uncertainty (varying environmental-ban standards)

blocks.text: Judicial activism, when rooted in constitutional fidelity and public interest, serves as a vital corrective to executive inaction and legislative inertia. Yet when it blurs into judicial adventurism, it risks eroding democratic accountability and unsettling the separation of powers.
